newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden and Britain more isolated with Italy in ERM.
newsitem.headline: Sweden and Britain more isolated with Italy in ERM.

text.p: Italy's entry into the EU's exchange rate mechanism leaves only Sweden, Britain and Greece outside the currency grid, further strengthening the majority view that a country must join to qualify for monetary union.
After Finland entered in October and Italy followed this weekend, the ERM groups 12 of the Union's 15 currencies.

Britain and Sweden have become increasingly isolated in arguing that currency stability, not ERM membership in itself, should be decisive for fulfilling the exchange rate requirement for joining economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"To keep the options open for EMU they would have to get into the ERM before the end of the year," said Bruce Kasman, head of European research at investment bank JP Morgan.
The currency criterion is one of five conditions which a country must meet to be allowed to join EMU. The others set limits on debt and borrowing, interest rates and inflation.
Kasman said that there has been a growing realisation over the last few months that ERM, which limits fluctuations between participating currencies, is a requirement for EMU.
However, there are no indications that either Stockholm or London would bow to any pressure and enter soon.
After Sunday's lira re-entry, Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink insisted this would not change anything for his country.
"Our attitude (on the ERM) has not changed because of today's decision," he told reporters.
British Treasury Minister Phillip Oppenheim told parliament last week: "The government has no intention of re-entering sterling in the exchange rate mechanism."

Robin Marshall, chief economist at Chase Manhattan in London, said Italy's ERM entry "highlights the increasing isolation of the U.K.," but that the issue was on the backburner, at least until the election which is to be held by May 1997.

Britain is divided over the single currency. The two major political parties -- the governing Conservatives and the opposition Labour party -- say they will decide later whether to exercise the country's opt out from the single currency.

In Sweden, Central Bank governor Urban Backstrom has indicated he would personally be in favour of joining the ERM, saying it would underline the increased stability of the economy. But he admits there is little support for such a move.

"We have made it perfectly clear that ERM membership is not being considered at present and will require broad support in the Swedish society," Backstrom said on Friday. "To date, however, the reactions have been hesitant."
Backstrom acknowledged this month that 13 out of the EU's 15 member states believe ERM is a necessary condition for EMU.
But he stressed that the final decision on the interpretation of the criterion would not be taken until early 1998 when EU leaders decide which countries qualify for EMU.

Kasman at JP Morgan said there was so much opposition to the single currency in Sweden that it was uncertain whether the Italian move would change anything. "But Sweden will be the country to watch between now and the end of the year."
Eric Chaney, senior economist at Morgan Stanley, said the Italian move might affect Sweden. "It will increase pressure and and will increase the probability that Sweden changes its mind."
Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter, saying Italy's entry would place Sweden "unpleasently clearly in the political periphery", urged the government to join the ERM quickly.
Greece, the third country outside the ERM, is in a different situation. The only country that has not fulfilled a single EMU requirement, Greece is an unlikely candidate for soon ERM entry.
